summary.value: This paper explains why soft-label regularizers (label smoothing, Mixup, CutMix) simultaneously improve calibration and adversarial robustness by analyzing the geometry of the representation space (penultimate-layer features). It shows that decision regions are effectively cone-shaped around the origin in high dimensions even with classifier biases (Section 3.1; Table 5, Table 6), and introduces confidence contours and loss-gradient directions that radiate from minimum-loss points (Fig. 2). The authors define class centers as minimum-loss points and demonstrate that feature alignment to these centers correlates best with confidence across architectures on ImageNet (Table 1). They prove and empirically verify that soft labels shrink feature norms (RMS) and increase alignment to class centers (Theorem 1; Figs. 4–6; Table 2), which reduces overconfidence in a way akin to temperature scaling (Section 4.3; Fig. 25). The analysis further links higher alignment to improved robustness against gradient-based attacks (FGSM, PGD, AutoAttack) and transfer-based black-box attacks (Section 4.4; Fig. 3 middle; Table 2; Table 4), and documents broader gains under natural corruptions (Table 3). The paper also clarifies why robustness gains taper under strong iterative attacks via trajectory analysis in the representation space (Appendix N; Fig. 13).

strengths.value:
1. Clear, original definition of class centers via minimum-loss points and strong validation. The paper argues that alignment should be measured to “the point where the classification loss is the lowest” rather than to the class mean or weight vector (Section 4.1). This choice is quantitatively justified: minimum-loss centers have the highest correlation with confidence across multiple architectures on ImageNet (Table 1), and the estimates are robust to optimization hyperparameters (Appendix I; Table 9). The 2D illustration makes the distinctions concrete (Fig. 2d).

2. Nontrivial geometric finding that cone-shaped decision regions persist in high dimensions even with classifier biases. Contrary to prior visualizations that omit bias, the authors provide a scalable verification method: linearly sweep features toward the origin and measure the first misclassification index (Appendix C). The indices are ≳99/100 across datasets and models (Table 5), and bias-dependence ratios n′c/nc are near zero (Table 6), supporting the claim in Section 3.1 without relying on 2D projections.

3. Introduction of confidence contours and gradient-direction fields in representation space that “radiate outward from the minimal-loss points,” exposing convex structure (Section 3.2). The visual analyses (Fig. 2a–c; Fig. 5) are novel, actionable, and directly connect feature norm and angular alignment to both calibration and adversarial gradients.

4. Theoretical grounding of the soft-label effect on feature norms. Theorem 1 (Appendix J) proves that soft-label training yields a finite optimal feature norm while hard-label training pushes norms to infinity. This theoretical claim is empirically borne out across architectures (Table 2; Figs. 4–6), providing a rare theory–practice bridge in representation geometry.

5. Unified mechanism linking calibration improvements to norm shrinkage, with a precise operational analogy to temperature scaling. Section 4.3 demonstrates that reducing feature RMS scales logits similarly to temperature scaling and improves calibration without changing accuracy; this is verified by manual feature scaling (Appendix L; Fig. 25) and reliability diagrams (Fig. 3 bottom).

6. Mechanistic and quantitative link from alignment to robustness across attack families. The paper shows bin-wise that higher cosine similarity to class centers lowers attack success for FGSM, PGD, and AutoAttack under weak and strong settings (Fig. 3 middle; Figs. 19–22; Table 2). The analysis extends beyond white-box settings to natural corruptions (ImageNet-C; Table 3) and transfer-based black-box attacks (Table 4), increasing practical significance.

7. Resolution of a subtle contradiction with an insightful, testable argument. Section 5 reconciles “closer to decision boundaries due to smaller RMS” with “more robust” by showing that (i) perturbation directions become inward for well-aligned features (Fig. 5a) and (ii) perturbation scale in representation space grows with feature RMS (positive correlation in Fig. 7). This is a crisp, empirically supported explanation rather than a heuristic claim.

8. Methodological contributions for high-dimensional verification. Besides the origin-sweep index (Appendix C), the paper introduces a simple bias-dependence diagnostic and reports small |bc| and n′c/nc in real high-D models (Appendix D; Table 6). These tools make otherwise hard-to-verify geometric claims reproducible without bespoke visualization tricks.

9. Breadth and consistency across architectures and training regimes. The main claims are tested on ResNet50, Swin-T, MobileNetV2, ConvNeXt-T, and ViT-B/16, with multiple soft-label regularizers (Label Smoothing, Mixup, CutMix) and even pretrained variants (Table 2; Table 8; Appendices K, E). The repeated observation—RMS↓ and cosine similarity↑—bolsters generality.

10. Transparent analysis of limitations with an explanatory trajectory view. The paper does not overclaim; it shows why gains diminish under stronger iterative attacks by visualizing how PGD trajectories turn outward after initial inward steps (Appendix N; Fig. 13). This candid, mechanistic account increases credibility.

11. Clarifying discussion on CNN vs. Transformer robustness/calibration under matched recipes. The controlled comparison suggests that, absent soft-label regularization, Swin-T is “as overconfident” and often more attack-susceptible than ResNet50 (Section A Discussion; Table 2), challenging a common narrative and attributing perceived advantages to training choices.

12. High pedagogical quality with precise visuals and “Key Takeaway” summaries. The narrative is easy to follow, with strong figure support (e.g., Fig. 1–2, 4–6) and a clear 2D/3D visualization pipeline (Appendix H). The paper balances intuition (confidence contours, gradient fields) and quantitative checks, making the insights accessible and verifiable.

weaknesses.value:
1. Limited theoretical grounding of the gradient-field and “class center” geometry beyond 2D
- Evidence: The convexity argument in Section 3.2 is correct for logits affine in features, but the key claim that “gradient directions radiate outward from the minimal-loss points” and organize regions into inward (toward origin) vs boundary-seeking flows is demonstrated in 2D (Fig. 2b–c; Fig. 5) and then used to reason in high dimensions. The uniqueness and location of the “minimum-loss points” are empirically established (Table 1; Appendix I) but lack a formal characterization.
- Actionable: Provide a high-dimensional characterization of the gradient field on low-dimensional linear subspaces anchored at real features, e.g., 2D planes spanned by (f, w_c) and by (f, nearest competing w_k), without retraining to 2D (see Appendix H). Validate that the inward-vs-boundary dichotomy and the identified centers persist on these slices across many samples. Prove (or bound) the existence/uniqueness of minimum-loss centers per class under mild assumptions (e.g., near-neural-collapse regimes).

2. Cone-shaped decision region claim relies on a heuristic test and shows notable deviations
- Evidence: The “move to origin” index is high but not near-perfect for some architectures on ImageNet (MobileNetV2: 91.3 ± 10.7; ConvNeXt-T: 93.9 ± 8.1; Table 5). The paper concludes “cone-shaped” regions in high-D even with bias (Section 3.1; Appendices C–D) but does not analyze when/why deviations occur.
- Actionable: Quantify angular decision boundaries directly by measuring argmax changes along angular sweeps at fixed radii around w_c, and correlate deviations with |b_c| and inter-class angle. Report per-class failure rates and their relation to calibration/robustness. This would convert the origin-sweep heuristic into a diagnostic that explains the residual non-cone behavior seen in Table 5.

3. Theorem 1 requires equal weight norms and does not address alignment
- Evidence: The norm-shrinkage result (Section 4.2; Appendix J) assumes ||w_c|| ≈ ||w|| (neural-collapse-like; Papyan et al., 2020). In practice, Table 6 shows heterogeneous |b_c| across models (e.g., MobileNetV2, ConvNeXt-T), and the theorem does not treat unequal norms nor explain the empirically central alignment increase (Section 4.2; Fig. 6; Table 2).
- Actionable: (i) Extend the analysis to unequal weight norms and nonzero biases to bound the gap between hard/soft solutions. (ii) Provide a complementary analysis for alignment: derive how smaller ||f|| tightens the angular band needed to reach a fixed confidence (Fig. 6) in high-D, and quantify expected cosine increases as a function of soft-label strength.

4. Calibration evaluation is narrow and conflates mechanisms with outcomes
- Evidence: Calibration is assessed mainly via ECE and reliability diagrams (Fig. 3 bottom; Table 2), and Section 4.3 claims feature scaling mimics temperature scaling, noting “bias values are close to zero.” Yet Table 6 shows sizeable mean |b_c| for MobileNetV2/ConvNeXt-T, which can make w⊤f/T + b_c differ materially from (w⊤f)/T + b_c/T.
- Actionable: (i) Report multiple metrics (NLL, Brier, adaptive-ECE) to ensure robustness of conclusions. (ii) Quantify the per-sample difference between temperature scaling and feature scaling in logits, show its distribution, and its impact on calibration metrics. (iii) Include a post-hoc temperature scaling baseline to separate the contribution of norm shrinkage from other effects.

5. Visualization pipeline retrains networks in 2D, risking geometry artifacts
- Evidence: Appendix H inserts a learned 2D (or 3D) bottleneck and trains end-to-end to visualize Fig. 1–2, 4, 9–12. This changes the representation learning objective and may induce geometry that does not exist in the trained high-D models.
- Actionable: Replace or complement 2D re-training with: (i) linear slices through the original high-D space as above; (ii) supervised LDA or random projections of high-D features to 2D/3D for visualization; (iii) per-sample local tangent analyses around high-D features to visualize gradient directions and confidence contours without altering training.

6. Robustness evaluation underestimates strong iterative attacks and lacks standard reporting
- Evidence: “Strong” PGD uses 7 steps with α=2/255 (Section 4.4; Table 2); this is short relative to standard PGD-50/100 setups. AutoAttack is included but only at two ε; robust accuracy is not reported (only ASR). Appendix N (Fig. 13) provides a qualitative trajectory explanation but no quantitative stress tests.
- Actionable: (i) Report robust accuracy vs ε curves, and include PGD-50/100, CW-L2, and Square Attack; (ii) provide gradient-obfuscation checks (loss landscape smoothness, BPDA/EOT for any non-differentiabilities); (iii) add per-bin results for stronger settings (as in Fig. 19–22) and quantify the alignment-robustness link under PGD-50.

7. Minimum-loss center estimation lacks computational analysis and practical surrogates
- Evidence: Centers are located by gradient descent (Section 4.1; Fig. 2d; Table 1), and stability is shown (Appendix I), but the computational overhead on ImageNet-scale models is not reported. For practitioners, weight vectors or class means are much cheaper.
- Actionable: (i) Report the runtime/compute to estimate centers per model; (ii) propose/validate approximations (e.g., radius-optimized points along w_c direction, or convex combinations of weight and class mean) that approach the correlation of Table 1 with much lower cost.

8. Soft-label training hyperparameters and convergence are not systematically explored
- Evidence: Training adopts a single Mixup/CutMix alpha (1.0) and LS=0.1 for ImageNet (Appendix G.2). ConvNeXt-T with CutMix “failed to converge” in Table 1. There is no sensitivity study linking soft-label strength to RMS, cosine alignment, ECE, and robustness.
- Actionable: Provide sensitivity curves over α and LS-ε for each architecture, reporting RMS↓, cosine↑, ECE, and robust accuracy. Diagnose and fix convergence issues (e.g., tuning α per architecture for ConvNeXt-T) to ensure fair comparisons.

9. Bias-related claims conflict and are under-quantified
- Evidence: Section 4.3 asserts bias is “close to zero,” but Table 6 shows larger |b_c| for MobileNetV2/ConvNeXt-T (means 0.339/0.463). The paper then infers temperature scaling ≈ feature scaling.
- Actionable: Explicitly quantify how often the difference between the two scalings changes the top-1 class. Report calibration/robustness deltas between the two scalings stratified by |b_c|. This would reconcile Section 4.3 with Table 6 and bound when the analogy holds.

10. Causal attribution for alignment improvements is not isolated from norm effects
- Evidence: Section 4.2 argues smaller ||f|| narrows angular regions for fixed confidence (Fig. 6), implying higher cosine. However, the alignment increase might be a byproduct of norm shrinkage rather than an independent driver of robustness (Section 4.4).
- Actionable: Add controlled experiments that (i) fix feature norms post hoc (normalize ||f|| to a common radius) and compare alignment distributions and ASR between baseline vs soft-label models; (ii) equalize confidence distributions via temperature scaling and examine whether alignment still explains residual robustness differences.

11. Perturbation scale vs feature RMS is correlational and may be confounded
- Evidence: Fig. 7 shows a positive correlation between feature RMS and perturbation RMS (for ε=8/255), used to argue that features near the origin “move less.”
- Actionable: Compute partial correlations controlling for the input gradient norm and per-class curvature; or stratify by gradient norm to show the relation is not an artifact. Report effect sizes and confidence intervals.

12. Generality beyond CE/linear heads and vision is asserted as future work but can be partially tested
- Evidence: Section 8 suggests extending to other losses/objectives. The current scope uses a standard linear head and cross-entropy.
- Actionable: Include small-scale validations with cosine classifiers (e.g., NormFace), focal loss, or MSE classification, and one non-vision dataset (e.g., speech commands) to probe whether cone regions, norm shrinkage, and alignment-robustness links persist.

13. Reporting choices obscure robustness and calibration trade-offs in pretrained comparisons
- Evidence: Table 8 shows that stronger regularization (e.g., MobileNetV2 V2) can drastically increase ECE (0.367) despite RMS↓ and cosine↑, which seems at odds with the main narrative.
- Actionable: Clarify whether ECE is signed or absolute (Fig. 3 uses color to indicate under/overconfidence), and add NLL/Brier to disentangle underconfidence vs overconfidence. Provide temperature-scaled baselines for those pretrained weights to show residual gaps attributable to representation changes rather than calibration alone.

questions.value:
1. High-dimensional gradient field and “class centers”
- In Section 3.2 and Fig. 2b–c you characterize gradient directions “radiating outward” from minimum-loss points using 2D models trained with a learned 2D bottleneck (Appendix H). Could you verify this geometry directly in the original high-D models by analyzing 2D linear subspaces without retraining, e.g., planes spanned by (f, w_y) and by (f, w_compete)? Reporting aggregate angular deviations from inward vs boundary-seeking directions on these slices would strengthen the high-D claim. Also, can you characterize existence/uniqueness of per-class minimum-loss points (beyond the empirical stability in Appendix I, Table 9)?

2. Extending Theorem 1 beyond equal-norm weights and connecting to alignment
- Theorem 1 (Section 4.2; Appendix J) assumes ||w_c|| ≈ ||w||. Table 6 shows heterogeneity in |b_c| (e.g., MobileNetV2, ConvNeXt-T). Can you extend the analysis to unequal weight norms and nonzero biases to bound the hard vs soft feature-norm gap? More importantly, can you quantify how decreased ||f|| tightens the angular band needed to reach a fixed confidence (Fig. 6) in high dimension, yielding a prediction for the expected cosine increase as a function of label-smoothing ε or Mixup α?

3. Cone-shaped regions: diagnosing deviations in high dimension
- The origin-sweep test in Appendix C yields lower indices for MobileNetV2 and ConvNeXt-T on ImageNet (Table 5: 91.3±10.7, 93.9±8.1). Could you (i) measure decision changes along angular sweeps at fixed radii around w_c to directly test cone behavior, (ii) report per-class failure rates, and (iii) correlate deviations with |b_c| and inter-class angles (Appendix D; Table 6)? This would clarify when/why non-cone deviations arise in high-D.

4. Feature scaling vs temperature scaling under non-negligible biases
- Section 4.3 argues feature scaling is similar to temperature scaling; yet Table 6 reports sizable |b_c| for some models. Please quantify the per-sample logit difference between feature scaling and temperature scaling, the frequency of top-1 changes, and the impact on calibration (NLL, Brier, adaptive-ECE), stratified by |b_c|. Adding a post-hoc temperature-scaling baseline would help disentangle the norm-shrinkage mechanism from generic logit scaling.

5. Visualization without retraining-induced geometry
- Because 2D/3D visualizations are produced by inserting and training a low-D linear layer (Appendix H), it would help to add complementary views from the original models: (i) random projections of high-D features, (ii) supervised LDA projections, and (iii) local gradient flow visualizations on 2D subspaces through original features (see Q1). Please also report whether the 2D-bottleneck models retain similar accuracy and ECE to their high-D counterparts to rule out learning artifacts.

6. Robustness under stronger iterative attacks and standard reporting
- Table 2 evaluates PGD with 7 steps and AutoAttack at two ε. For a fuller picture, could you provide: (i) robust accuracy vs ε curves; (ii) PGD-50/100 and CW-L2 (or Square Attack) results; (iii) gradient-obfuscation checks (e.g., loss landscape smoothness, BPDA/EOT if any non-differentiabilities)? Also extend the per-bin alignment analysis (Fig. 19–22) to PGD-50 to validate that higher cosine still correlates with robustness under stronger optimization.

7. Causal role of alignment vs norm shrinkage
- Section 4.4 attributes robustness to improved alignment. To isolate alignment from norm effects, could you add: (i) a post-hoc normalization that equalizes ||f|| across models (e.g., renormalize features to a common radius) and compare ASR/robust accuracy and cosine distributions; (ii) equalize confidence distributions via temperature scaling and test whether alignment still explains robustness differences?

8. Perturbation RMS vs feature RMS (Fig. 7): controls and effect sizes
- Please report the partial correlation between perturbation RMS and feature RMS when controlling for input gradient norm and class. Also show results at multiple ε and with PGD to confirm the relation is not attack-specific. Confidence intervals or bootstraps for correlation coefficients would make effect sizes clearer.

9. Minimum-loss center estimation: compute and surrogates
- Section 4.1 and Appendix I do not quantify the computational cost of estimating centers on ImageNet. Please report runtime/compute and propose practical surrogates (e.g., optimizing along w_c only, or convex combinations of weight vector and class mean). How close do these surrogates get to the Table 1 correlations?

10. Sensitivity to soft-label hyperparameters and convergence issues
- Appendix G.2 fixes LS=0.1 and α=1.0 for Mixup/CutMix on ImageNet, and Table 1 notes a CutMix failure to converge for ConvNeXt-T. Could you provide sensitivity curves over LS ε and α for each architecture, reporting RMS, cosine, ECE, and robust accuracy, and diagnose the ConvNeXt-T/CutMix failure (e.g., learning rate, mix probability, label mixing strategy)?

11. Reconciling bias claims and calibration examples
- Section 4.3 states “most bias values are close to zero,” but Table 6 shows larger |b_c| for MobileNetV2/ConvNeXt-T. Please reconcile these statements and quantify how often bias magnitudes materially affect the feature-vs-temperature scaling equivalence and calibration outcomes.

12. Pretrained weight anomalies and calibration metrics
- In Table 8, stronger-regularized variants (e.g., MobileNetV2 V2, EfficientNet-B1 V2) have RMS↓ and cosine↑ yet much higher ECE (likely underconfidence). Could you clarify whether ECE is signed vs absolute (Fig. 3 bottom uses color), and add NLL/Brier/Adaptive-ECE to show the full calibration picture? Also compare to post-hoc temperature scaling on these checkpoints.

13. Generality beyond CE/linear heads and vision
- Section 8 lists this as future work. Could you include small-scale probes with a cosine classifier (e.g., NormFace), focal loss, or MSE classification, and one non-vision dataset (even a small speech/NLP classification task), to test whether cone-shaped regions, norm shrinkage, and alignment–robustness links persist?

14. Relationship among weight vectors, class means, and centers
- Fig. 2d and Table 1 show that weight vectors can be poor proxies for centers in some classes. Can you provide per-class angular scatterplots between these three candidates and analyze when/why weights deviate (e.g., class imbalance, |b_c|, inter-class angles)? This would help practitioners choose center surrogates when computing true centers is expensive.

15. Natural corruptions (Table 3): normalization and per-severity analyses
- To separate gains from clean-accuracy differences, could you report mCE normalized by each model’s clean error (as in Hendrycks & Dietterich), and include per-severity curves for a few representative corruptions to illustrate how RMS↓ and cosine↑ translate into robustness across severity levels?
